name: Coaching Students Through Primary Sources
title: Coaching Students Through Primary Sources
answer: Coaching students through primary sources means using a school configured AI tool as a question asking coach rather than as an interpreter of the material. The tool prompts students with the questions a historian would ask, and the student does the reading, the reasoning and the writing. It matters because reading primary sources well is a skill built over years, and a tool that hands over the meaning would remove the very practice students need.

crumbs.name: Social Studies, Civics, and World Languages

sections.body: Primary sources are the raw material of history, and they include letters, speeches, photographs and government records. Reading them well is a skill students build over years, not something they acquire in a single lesson. AI can help students work with these sources without doing the interpreting for them. A school configured tool acts as a coach, asking the questions a historian would ask, such as who created the document and when, what the author was trying to accomplish, what it leaves out, and who might see it differently. The student answers, the coach asks follow up questions, and the tool never tells the student what the source means.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The approach fits naturally with document based questions. A teacher can set up a hint only tool, as described in Chapter 7, that helps students plan an essay using a set of documents without writing the essay for them. The tool might ask which documents support the student's argument and which complicate it, leaving the reading, the reasoning and the writing to the student. The supplied text does not give grade bands for this practice, so it is described here as a general approach rather than one tied to particular year groups. Teachers choose the sources themselves, and the coach then helps students read those real sources.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers no study, figure or finding for this idea, and it carries no evidence label. It rests on practice rather than research. What the text does point to is the availability of material, noting that the Library of Congress and many state archives offer large collections of primary sources free of charge. It also refers to the hint only tool described in Chapter 7 as a workable pattern for document based questions. Beyond those practical references, no research base is claimed.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets clear limits. Teachers should choose the sources themselves, because AI tools can suggest documents but sometimes describe documents that do not exist or misquote real ones. Every source students use should come from an archive, a library database or a trusted collection, so that the coach helps students read real sources rather than invented ones. The interpreting stays with the student, since the tool asks questions but does not supply meaning. The reading, the reasoning and the writing remain the student's work, and the choice of documents remains the teacher's decision.
